title: Weight-Space Micromachines: Brain Implants for LLMs
author: dataminer

excerpt: TL;DR AI agents can write small modules ("implants") straight into weight space and bolt them onto a frozen LLM: a calculator, "eyes" for images, a mistake detector, a little memory that lets the model retry a problem and vote inside one call. Implants stay OFF until needed, so the model is bit-for-bit unchanged until one fires. Attaching them alone climbs benchmarks like RL but without RL: on Qwen3-0.6B-Base, BIG-Bench Hard goes from 41% to 55%, IFEval from 13% to 35%. You can also RL with implants attached: on GSM8K, RL with implants reaches 80% vs 68% for plain RL, BIG-Bench Hard 60% vs 54% and IFEval 48% vs 46%. Code: github.com/anadim/weight-space-micromachines. Today, teaching a language model a new skill means fine-tuning or RL on data that exercises it, and hoping nothing else breaks, or wrapping the model in tools, sandboxes and parsers. What if instead you could write the skill straight into the model's weights? Like having an exact co-processor that comes with the model, stays off until it's needed, one that can even be trained/RL'd along with it? This was an old wish of mine! In 2023, in Looped Transformers as Programmable Computers [1], Angeliki and Shashank hand picked the weights of a transformer and put it in a loop so that the model could run programs (a calculator, a computer, a full blown gradient descent run in context!). The process was quite painful, but the results were cute and the "looped transformer" name stuck around :). At some point in the paper we wrote (verbatim): we hope that our findings will contribute to the development of methods to enhance the capabilities of trained language models by utilizing smaller, reverse-engineered transformer networks for specific algorithmic tasks We really wanted to do this back then, but handwriting even small circuits was painful, especially ones working in token space that then had to be attached to a bigger model.
